items.title: Cognitive Biases
items.content: **Bias distinctions:** Availability concerns ease of retrieval; representativeness concerns similarity to a prototype; anchoring concerns insufficient adjustment; framing concerns presentation-dependent choice; confirmation bias concerns preferential search or interpretation. Dunning-Kruger findings concern calibration under particular tasks and measures, not a rule that every low performer is overconfident. One judgment does not diagnose a bias or ability.

items.title: Defense Mechanisms
items.content: **Psychodynamic defense cue:** Repression, denial, projection, displacement, reaction formation, intellectualization, and sublimation are hypotheses about how affect or conflict may be managed. Proposed maturity groupings are dimensional theoretical formulations, not a fixed diagnostic ladder. The same observable behavior can serve different functions, so context, alternatives, development, culture, and the person's experience must guide interpretation.

items.title: Bandura's Social Learning
items.content: **Observational-learning sequence:** Attention, retention, behavioral production, and motivation help organize whether modeled behavior is acquired and expressed. Observing a model can teach a response without immediate imitation, and reinforcement often affects performance rather than being necessary for acquisition. Self-efficacy draws on mastery, vicarious experience, social persuasion, and physiological or affective information; no source is universally strongest.

items.title: Sternberg's & Gardner's Intelligence
items.content: **Theory comparison:** Sternberg's triarchic account emphasizes analytical, creative, and practical adaptation; Gardner proposed multiple relatively distinct intelligences. These frameworks broaden questions beyond conventional test content, but categories are theoretical and their measurement evidence differs. They do not show that standard cognitive tests measure nothing important or that every talent is an independent intelligence. Use current test manuals for score interpretation.

items.title: Language Development Theories
items.content: **Competing language accounts:** Behaviorist, nativist, statistical-learning, social-interaction, usage-based, and connectionist approaches emphasize different learning inputs and mechanisms. Children's productive errors and novel-word performance show generalization beyond exact imitation, but do not uniquely prove a language-acquisition device or rule out learning. Sensitive periods, input, interaction, cognition, and neurodevelopment all require evidence-bounded consideration.

items.title: Signal Detection Theory
items.content: **Signal-detection cue:** Sensitivity, commonly summarized by d-prime under model assumptions, separates distributions; response criterion reflects willingness to say "signal present." Hits, misses, false alarms, and correct rejections jointly determine interpretation. Payoffs, prevalence, instructions, fatigue, and expectations can shift criterion without changing sensitivity. The framework does not make every response a conscious decision or remove distributional assumptions.

items.title: Weber's & Fechner's Laws
items.content: **Psychophysics cue:** Weber's fraction describes approximately proportional just-noticeable differences over limited stimulus ranges; Fechner's logarithmic relation follows from additional assumptions about accumulating equal subjective steps. Neither is exact across every modality, intensity, or person. Method, adaptation, baseline level, and modern power-law alternatives matter, so use them as historical quantitative models rather than universal sensory laws.

items.title: Levels of Processing
items.content: **Encoding-depth cue:** Semantic or elaborative processing often supports later retention better than shallow structural processing under comparable conditions. "Depth" describes operations at encoding, not a literal place or fixed store, and memory also depends on retrieval cues, transfer-appropriate processing, organization, distinctiveness, prior knowledge, attention, and test format. One task cannot establish an enduring learning style.

items.title: Classical Conditioning Key Terms
items.content: **Conditioning terms:** An unconditioned stimulus elicits an unconditioned response without the target training; pairing can make a conditioned stimulus predict that outcome and evoke a conditioned response. Acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization, and discrimination describe measured patterns, not erasure or conscious choice. Timing, contingency, context, prior learning, and biological preparedness qualify simple pairing rules.

items.title: Stress & Coping Models
items.content: **Appraisal-and-coping cue:** Transactional models distinguish appraisal of demands and resources from coping efforts. Problem-focused and emotion-focused strategies are not inherently good or bad; fit depends on controllability, timing, goals, culture, safety, and consequences. Avoidance may reduce distress briefly yet maintain some problems, while acceptance can be adaptive without implying resignation. Stress responses are not uniform or purely cognitive.

items.title: Gestalt Principles of Perception
items.content: **Perceptual-organization cue:** Proximity, similarity, continuity, closure, common fate, and figure-ground relations describe tendencies in how elements are grouped. Stimulus arrangement, attention, task, learning, and context can change which organization dominates.

items.title: Depth Perception Cues
items.content: **Depth-cue map:** Binocular disparity and convergence depend on information from both eyes; motion parallax, occlusion, relative size, texture gradient, height, and linear perspective can operate monocularly. items.title: Attention Models
items.content: **Attention-model comparison:** Early-selection, attenuation, late-selection, capacity, and feature-integration accounts explain different task findings. Personally salient information may capture attention for some people and conditions; task load, expectations, timing, and individual differences matter.

items.title: Problem-Solving Barriers
items.content: **Problem-solving cue:** Functional fixedness limits alternative object uses; mental set carries a previously successful strategy forward; anchoring biases adjustment; heuristics trade completeness for efficiency. Algorithms are defined procedures, but only guarantee a solution when correctly specified, feasible, and applied to a problem in their scope. Expertise can help or constrain depending on representation; one failure does not diagnose "expertise blindness."

items.title: Signal Detection Theory
items.content: **Sensitivity versus criterion:** Signal detection theory models overlapping noise and signal-plus-noise distributions. Sensitivity indexes separation under assumptions; criterion reflects the response threshold shaped by base rate, payoff, instruction, and expectation. A higher hit rate alone cannot establish better sensitivity because false alarms matter. Measures and optimal thresholds depend on the specified model and consequences.

items.title: Bandura's Observational Learning
items.content: **Modeling cue:** Observational learning involves attending to a model, retaining information, being able to produce the response, and having conditions that motivate performance. Acquisition can occur without direct reinforcement, while observed consequences can alter whether behavior is expressed. Bobo-doll findings demonstrate modeled aggression under particular laboratory conditions, not inevitable imitation or a complete account of real-world aggression.

items.title: Classical Conditioning Phenomena
items.content: **Conditioning phenomena:** Extinction is new learning that reduces responding when the conditioned cue no longer predicts the outcome; it does not necessarily erase acquisition. Spontaneous recovery, renewal, and reinstatement show context and time effects. Generalization spreads responding to similar cues; discrimination differentiates them. Blocking, overshadowing, and latent inhibition show that contingency, attention, and prior learning matter beyond simple pairing.

items.title: Memory Systems Taxonomy
items.content: **Memory-system cue:** Working memory supports temporary maintenance and manipulation; episodic and semantic memory are commonly grouped as explicit or declarative; skills, priming, and conditioning are commonly grouped as implicit or nondeclarative. items.title: Theories of Emotion
items.content: **Emotion-theory comparison:** James-Lange emphasizes perception of bodily change; Cannon-Bard historically emphasized parallel central and bodily responses; two-factor theory combines arousal with situational interpretation; appraisal accounts emphasize evaluations. These are organizing contrasts, not complete current neural sequences. Emotion can involve appraisal, action tendencies, bodily signals, learning, culture, and context, and no vignette proves one mechanism exclusively.

items.title: Intelligence Theories
items.content: **Intelligence-framework cue:** Spearman proposed general and specific factors; Cattell-Horn distinguished broad abilities including fluid and crystallized knowledge; CHC organizes hierarchical broad and narrow abilities; Sternberg and Gardner proposed broader functional accounts. "Culture-free," fixed age decline, and independent-intelligence claims are too absolute. Theory, test construction, validity evidence, opportunity, language, education, and uncertainty must be separated.
